utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now for the Defence, please, who are complete today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Mr. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good morning to all those present: To the representatives of the Prosecution, assisted by their legal assistant; the Defence attorneys, as I have just said, are all present today; the accused; and all the personnel of this courtroom, especially the registrar, the legal officer, Madam Usher, Madam Court Reporter, as well as the security services. I will not omit to mention the interpreters in their booths. I would like to ask the registrar that we first go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mundis, is your witness available to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: He is indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to ask Madam Usher to go and fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that you are hearing my words in your own language. If so, tell me, please, that you can hear and understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called by representatives of the Prosecution to testify on certain matters linked to documents. Before I ask you to read the solemn declaration, I need to know your identity. Give me your first and last name, place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Mekic Muradif, born on the 13th of March, 1944, in Mrdjenovici, Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation? Are you working or are you retired? What are you doing now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you retired as what, from what position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a professional officer in the Yugoslav People's Army, a lieutenant colonel by rank in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when did you retire, which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And since 1997 you haven't been working. You are just a pensioner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was the position that you held in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? What was your position and rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I still didn't have any rank. Only the corps commanders were granted ranks, and senior officers. In those days, until mid-1993, I acted as chief of staff of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina headquartered in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the chief of staff of the 3rd Corps had no military rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was he considered to be an officer or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was considered to be an officer, a member of the Supreme Command, with a certain insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 or is this the first time for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is for the first time that I am appearing as a witness ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the text of the solemn declaration now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin with your testimony - I can call you Colonel because you are a retired colonel - I shall provide you with some information regarding these proceedings. You will have to answer questions that are going to be put to you by the representatives of the Prosecution, who are seated on your right. I understand that you have already met representatives of the Prosecution on several occasions and most recently this morning in the presence of the Defence attorneys. After the Prosecution's questions, the Defence attorneys, who are seated on your left and whom you have already met, will also have questions to you within the framework of their cross-examination. The Chamber understands that the Defence had intended to call you later as a witness for the Defence, but due to certain problems linked to documents, the Prosecution has called you to come and testify about some documents and the question of the chain of custody of documents within the 3rd Corps and questions linked to communications. Once the Defence attorneys have completed their questioning about the points I have just listed, the Prosecution may again have some additional questions for you. When this is over, the three Judges who are seated in front of you may also ask you questions. In view of the technical nature of your testimony, it is almost certain that the Judges will have questions for you. The questions put to you will be worded in a clear and understandable fashion as far as possible, and please try and answer them also clearly so as to inform the Judges fully of what you are saying. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, please ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it so that you are fully aware and understand the question which will allow you to give a precise answer. However, I have to remind you - and this is something that I do for all witnesses, not just for you but all those coming to testify - I need to remind witnesses that as they have taken the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, all false testimony is excluded. I always tell witnesses that should there be any false testimony, a witness may be sanctioned by a fine or a prison term which can go up to seven years. That is the first point. The second point I need to make is that when a witness has to answer a question which he considers that might one day be used against him because his answer may incriminate him, in that case the witness may refuse to answer. This is a possibility that exists in a number of countries. The witness is not forced to answer, but should that occur, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer, but in doing so, the Chamber guarantees immunity from prosecution to the witness for what the witness may say. Those would be, in general terms, how these proceedings will evolve. Should you have any difficulty, please tell us so and we will deal with them. I now turn to the Prosecution and give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning for the second time today, Mr. Mekic. As we explained --

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As we explained to you both in Sarajevo and earlier this morning, my questions, as you're aware, will be limited to technical issues concerning orders, and I will also show you a few documents, as we've previously done. Let me start by asking you, sir, you've informed the Trial Chamber that in 1992 you were a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Can you tell us, please, when you first joined the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I joined the JNA as an active-duty officer on the 27th of July, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you remained with the JNA until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was your military specialisation, if any, during your nearly 30-year career in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: My speciality was nuclear, chemical and biological defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the circumstances by which you left the JNA in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: If I may provide an explanation before I answer that question, please. The Yugoslav People's Army consisted of three components; the Yugoslav People's Army itself, the Territorial Defence, and the police in wartime. So only in wartime does the police become a third component. I think it was on the 13th of February, 1991, at my personal request I was transferred to serve in the Territorial Defence as a component of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, and I held the position of assistant commander for logistics of the District TO staff for Sarajevo. You are probably aware of the fact that the commander was General Jovan Divjak. I held that post until the 4th of April, 1992, when we were called on either to move to where the occupier, as we thought them to be, should go or to leave. Those of us who were professional officers decided not to join the armed forces that had been formed by the JNA - I don't know how to put it - the forces whose task it was to ensure the -- to ensure that Bosnia-Herzegovina remain in Rump Yugoslavia. As far as the Bosnian and Croatian patriots in the Territorial Defence were concerned, we remained there, but not under the command of the Main Staff over which the JNA had command. This lasted only four days. On the 8th of April, 1992, an order was issued by the then Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the patriotic forces should unite to form the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and those patriotic forces were the Patriotic League and the Territorial Defence. So that from the Territorial Defence, for four days I was nowhere, so to speak, and then, together with the others, I joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point, 8 April 1992, what were you assigned to do and where were you?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo, in the district of Ciglane, where the District TO headquarters was based, and we stayed there. I was a member of the staff without any concrete duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the district of Ciglane in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I was there until the Marsal Tito barracks was liberated, if you're aware of that event. You probably are. When the barracks was liberated, I was appointed the first commander of that barracks, the assignment being to prepare the area to accommodate the growing units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long -- how long, sir, did you remain in Sarajevo in 1992 -- or, better, when did you leave Sarajevo in 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I left Sarajevo -- actually, I wasn't alone. Four of us left Sarajevo in the night between the 1st and 2nd of November, 1992, escorted by the French colonel who escorted us via the airport, and then we continued on our way to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was with you on this trip to Zenica and what the purpose of going to Zenica was on the 1st and 2nd of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: In the group with me was Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic, Velaga Karajko, and Mikic Senad. The purpose of our leaving Sarajevo and going to Central Bosnia, or more specifically to Zenica, was to implement the plan Koverat, or envelope as it was code named, and the name of that plan was to lift the blockade of the city of Sarajevo. The four of us were assigned to go to Central Bosnia to organise units there, and with those units to start the operation of deblocking Sarajevo from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As part of this tasking to organise these units, did that include the establishment of a corps?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when that assignment, in effect, turned into the establishment of a corps?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, on the 2nd of November, in the evening, we arrived in Zenica. After life in surrounded Sarajevo and living under unbearable conditions -- I find it hard even to look back at that period, because I remember some horrific events. We felt as if we had reached another planet. The war could not be felt to such an extent in Zenica. There was lighting, which is something we were impressed by. Even traffic lights were working. Unfortunately, that same evening we were unpleasantly surprised, and only then did we realise the kind of media blockade we were under and general blockade, a lack of information and lack of knowledge about events. We had expected, according to certain information that we had received, that in Central Bosnia that units had already been organised which simply now had to be prepared for the execution of the assigned task. Unfortunately, none of that existed. All that existed was the 1st Zenica Brigade which existed on paper only. There was just one battalion that could actually be put to use consisting of the workers from the steelworks. Several days later, when we had an overview of the situation and when we saw that we could not carry out the task for which we had left Sarajevo, we addressed our superior command and informed them about the situation there such as it was. We gave up the plan called Koverat for Central Bosnia, and we were tasked to consolidate the units and to organise them and to undertake the establishment of the 3rd of -- 3rd Banja Luka or Krajina Corps based in Zenica. That is how it was known at first as the Krajina was occupied. But the first option was that it should be called the Banja Luka Corps. However, as that did not materialise, it remained to be called the 3rd Corps without any indication of place; that is, Banja Luka was left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, I appreciate that you have a great deal of knowledge on these matters, but again, due to the limited nature of the questions that I'll put to you, if you could try to keep the answers as brief as possible, that would be appreciated. Do you recall the approximate time that the 3rd Corps or the 3rd Banja Luka Corps or the Banja Luka Corps was established, the rough time period?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. As a professional soldier, I know that even in peacetime, under normal conditions, to form a corps requires a number of years. This is something you can check with military experts. But in wartime, well, we managed to do something. We gathered some units, but technically speaking, as far as the formation of a corps is concerned, that was out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, the question was the approximate time period when the 3rd Corps came into being.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, on paper it came into being perhaps in the first half of January 1992. I apologise: In 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was your position at the time the corps came into being?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the staff of the Supreme Command, and I went to Central Bosnia in order to deal with these affairs. I was a member of the staff of the Supreme Command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you told us that you were the chief of staff of the 3rd Corps until approximately mid-1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us very briefly what your responsibilities as chief of staff included.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I know you asked me that question a minute ago, because the corps commander and the chief of staff of the corps couldn't appoint themselves to those positions. That's why I said I was a member of the staff of the Supreme Command and that I wasn't the chief of staff until I received the order appointing me to that position. All this functioned on the basis of temporary orders. These appointments were temporary. They weren't real appointments. I'm not sure. I can't remember the date when the then Presidency issued the decrees and when I became the chief. I'm not sure of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, sir: What, briefly, were your duties and responsibilities as the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: You want brief answers, but it's not possible to answer that question by providing you with a brief answer. The staff was supposed to deal with the operational functions of the corps command, and that's why you have the chiefs of the services, and that the suggestion -- rather, the decision of the commander, combat operations would be prepared. Not just combat operations but life -- the life and work of the corps would also be organised on that basis. So I had a group of people with whom I was to implement the orders issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about how orders issued by the commander were created, the written orders. How was that process done?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two possibilities. Work was carried out on the basis of two written instructions, textbooks, so to speak. One of these textbooks, or some of these instructions had to do with office work and drafting official documents, and the other instructions had to do with the work of the staff. The working methods involved a lengthy procedure and a more rapid procedure. This depended on the situation and the time we had at our disposal. For a document or an order from a commander, let's say to attack or to defend, to go on a march, to rest, et cetera, for such an order to be implemented, all his associates would sit down together and discuss a number of issues, and the main issues that were discussed on the basis of which a document was drafted, this concerned the situation in the field, the combat situation, the time at our disposal, the weather, an assessment of the enemy. And once all that had been done, these evaluations were forwarded to the commander and the commander would then take a decision, and on the basis of his decision, a document would then be prepared. As I have already said, the combat order was the main document, the combat order for any kind of combat operation. It was on the basis of that order that other subsidiary documents were drafted. So for each combat operation drafted by a corps, a plan would be made which was fairly lengthy. Naturally within that framework everyone had his own duties. The logistics officer had to suggest the best kind of logistical support. The operations officers were those who suggested how the unit should be used in the field. The communications officer was, let's say the person who was the chief of the communications, his duty was to establish a communications system. And that's how this was done. Transport officers had to deal with transport, et cetera. And once they had made all these suggestions, then the order would be drafted, and one single plan would be made concerning the action that had to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there a specific person or persons within the 3rd Corps who were responsible for actually writing the orders?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was that person or persons?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: These were officers involved in operations, and at the beginning we had one computer. Only one computer was used initially, and this person who was typing out the handwritten text of operations officer -- or operations officers who drafted the documents would type out the document on this computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the document was typed out, I assumed it -- I assume it would then be printed out.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would be done with the document once it was printed from the computer?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The document would then be registered -- or, rather, first the relevant organ would sign it and then it was registered. It would be given a number, it would be stamped, and it was then taken to the communications centre. And it was supposed to be sent from the communications centre to the person to whom the document was addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that first the relevant organ would sign it. Who -- what do you mean by the "relevant organ" in terms of signing orders?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's specified on the basis of the hierarchy. This was something that had been established in the chain of command. Everything that was done was done on the basis of a commander's orders. As I said, the idea was that there should be a single command, and the commander was the person who would issue orders for everything. If the document was of a logistical kind, if it had to do with supporting provisions, food, et cetera, then naturally the assistant commander for logistics would sign such a document. If the document had to do with security or morale, then another person would sign it, the person who had to deal with this. This took place within the corps command. If it was an operations document, a report, a report that had been received, et cetera, then it would either be signed by the commander or I would sign it if the commander wasn't there. I would sign it as the chief of staff. And the document would then be sent -- or, rather, first it would be registered and then it would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us about a number of assistant chiefs of staff for these various departments who would sign documents. Would they be signing on behalf of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: In the system of control and command that we had adopted -- as I said, we didn't invent anything, we adopted the system from the JNA, from the former JNA. According to those instructions, the commander would sign -- or, rather, one would sign with the authorisation of the commander. For example, the person who was the assistant commander for staff, let's take that as an example, he would sign documents with the authorisation of the commander. So, for example, when it's -- when you have the commander's name, it would say "authorised by the commander," and his assistant for those affairs would sign at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Whose name would be typewritten or computer written on the document when these other individuals would sign?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: If it had to do with a given department, then you'd have to have the name of the chief of that department. For example, it would be the assistant commander for logistics or the assistant commander for the operations and staff affairs or the assistant commander for security or the assistant commander for morale, the assistant commander for security, for intelligence, et cetera. So these were assistant commanders, the chiefs of the sections who were involved in these affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a slightly different but related question. Documents bearing the signature block, if you will, the typewritten signature block of the commander of the corps, who was authorised to sign documents that included the commander's name, typewritten name, on the document?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Again I'll go back to what I was saying. According to the rules of control and command that had been adopted, there was the deputy commander who didn't require any particular kind of authorisation in order to sign on behalf of the commander if the commander was absent. And the others, if this was -- if this was something that took place outside of their departments, others required authorisation from the commander to sign such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what about the chief of staff, the position that you yourself held for a number of months? Could you sign on behalf of the commander in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: And also if the deputy commander was absent, then I was in a position to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So in effect, as chief of staff at that time in the 3rd Corps, you were the number three in the chain of command within the corps?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would -- who would sign the documents if the commander, the deputy commander, and the chief of staff were all absent? Did anyone have authority in that circumstance to sign documents on behalf of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of control and command, he didn't have authorisation to do that if he hadn't received written authorisation from the commander. But I'm not sure, I do think such things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So in effect, the commander could always authorise senior officers within the staff of the corps to sign on his behalf in his absence and in the absence of the deputy commander and chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: He could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to the issue of, in effect, certification or verification of orders prior to the orders going to the communications centre for transmittal to subordinate units. Are you familiar with that process?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So let's start with the moment the commander or an authorised person on behalf of the commander signs a written order. That document is then taken where?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That document would be taken to the so-called office -- the general services office. That's where we had a protocol, or, rather, a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. register, and the document would be registered there under a certain number. I don't want to repeat what I've already said. Various numbers, the main numbers were allocated, and once the document had been stamped and numbered, it would then be sent to the communications centre where they had a logbook there, a transmission logbook. That's what it was called. And they would make a note that the document had been received to be sent. They would write down the time it had been received, and they would write down the time it had been sent. They also would write down whether it had been sent, because quite frequently it was not possible to send a document; the document would be returned to the general services office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus your attention on that actual process of stamping the document. Can you tell us a little bit more about how that was done and the steps taken within the general services office to do that.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, I can't tell you exactly what procedure was followed, but I can tell you the procedure that should have been followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like you to tell me what should have been followed and then maybe we'll ask you about why that procedure wasn't always followed.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The person who typed the document out, who processed the document on a computer, having completed that work, and later on we received a computer, this was recorded on a floppy disk. Before we received computers, these documents were on paper. This would then be handed over to someone in the 3rd Corps. While I was there, there were two persons who would take turns. There were two women who were authorised. I won't say that they had taken an oath, but they had an obligation which was the case for all other members of the armed forces. They had the solemn obligation to perform those duties correctly and to take security measures, et cetera. The room itself was a large room, and by those persons who were involved in this, there was a partition. No one could gain access to where the documents and stamps were kept, et cetera. They couldn't approach them behind their backs. That's how things should have been. But as to whether someone ever did pass by them, I cannot say. They had three stamps on paper, and by those stamps you had the signatures of people who had the right to use stamps. So only documents with their signatures could be stamped. And if -- with regard to other people, if they had no authorisation for stamps to accompany their signatures, then this couldn't be done. And I don't know whether you asked me about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you a few follow-on questions from what you've told us. The document would arrive in the general services office and someone there would verify the signature against a known signature of the person who had signed the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps at the beginning until they got used to the signatures. Later on they knew exactly who had signed the document, so it wasn't necessary to always compare the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you've told us that there were three stamps. Can you tell us a little bit more about these three different stamps.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: There were three stamps, and it said the "3rd Corps Command" on the stamps. Stamp number one should be used next to the commander's signature since he was the first in command. Number two had to do with the deputy commander. Number three should have been for the chief of staff. I think the small numbers on the stamps can be seen. I think they're visible. You can see number 1, number 2, and number 3 when a document is stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've also told us -- let me retract that. What colour was the ink that was used to stamp the documents?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: It was the colour we managed to get hold of. Ink -- I don't know what they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour or colours were used by the 3rd Corps general services office during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really sure. I think that, as I said, we used what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask: You earlier alluded to a difference between how the procedure was supposed to work and how it may not have always worked that way. Can you tell us a little bit more about why the system, the regulations, weren't always followed?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Again, I would have to provide you with a -- a lengthy answer, and time is limited. This was, above all, the result of the fact that there were very few of us who were professionals. We were totally handicapped as far as the staff in the corps was concerned, as far as professional and educated people were concerned. Given the circumstances, we used the people we thought were the most capable. We had taxi drivers who had only finished primary school who would be a brigade commander. This should be understood. That is one of the reasons. People hadn't been educated or trained for those duties, and as a result there were certain errors, certain omissions; and secondly, the conditions under which we had to work were extremely difficult. The communications means were not adequate, almost non-existent. And later on when we obtained certain equipment, I think that 75 to 80 per cent of the time we remained without electricity. So we would obtain generators to solve the problem. And once we had obtained these generators, we would wait for UNPROFOR to supply us with fuel. So we didn't have fuel either. I could go on about this. It would take me a lot of time to explain the situation to you. It was an impossible situation to be in. We did all we could to resolve the problems we faced. And security was at a very low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you just a couple of final questions and then I'm going to show you some documents. Once the written order went through this entire process of being certified and stamped, you told us it was taken to the communications centre where it would be transmitted and certain stamps would be placed on it indicating the means by which it was transmitted. What would happen with the original order after that? What would -- where would it go from the com centre?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The original order, according to the regulations in force, should be returned to the general services department, where it would be stamped again in the top corner, indicating that it should be preserved until so-and-so. A combat document would have to be preserved for one, two, three, or five years, or permanently, because the archives were also in the general services department. So the document, after being sent, would be returned there for safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a little bit about the format or template, if you will, that was used for creating written orders. I'd like to focus your attention on the information at the upper left portion of a written order. Do you remember what information would be contained in the upper left part of an order?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. What should be stated on top would be "3rd Corps Command" -- or, rather, before that it should the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the 3rd Corps, then a number, the registration number, then the date when the document was drafted, and then, below that, a brief indication of what the document is. Is it an order? Is it a report or something like that? That should be stated there. Then in the same line, to the right, the addressees, and again the content. And in the top right-hand corner, military secret, confidential, strictly confidential, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to show you a number of documents with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, these are from among the original documents which I signed out from the legal officer. If the witness could please be shown contested document 329, and I would ask that that document please be placed on the ELMO. If the ELMO could be perhaps zoomed out slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise on this document -- sir, do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at the stamp to the left of your signature. And again, sir, if need be if you could actually turn and look at the actual document, that might be a little bit easier than staring at the screen. And perhaps if you could be given something to point with. You told us earlier, sir, that there were three stamps that were used within the corps. Do you see any particular features of this stamp that you've told us about previously?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: This is one of the three stamps that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us -- you told us, sir, that there were different stamps for the commander, deputy commander, and chief of staff. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that that is how it should have been. But whether that was observed or not, I can't say. I don't know. So that was up to the person who was actually doing the stamping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. And perhaps if you could now look at the screen where we've zoomed in on the stamp. Do you see which stamp is actually on this document?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. On the stamp there are two number 3s. Can you please, on the original to your left, point to the number 3.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does that 3 indicate?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does the small number 3 immediately above the letter R in Korpus indicate?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That would be the number 3 type of stamp. Because there's my signature, so then my stamp should have been used as well. I only say mine conditionally, but it was used for operative affairs in the operations department. So that stamp, that particular stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the stamp with the number 3 would be used for documents that you signed, or for documents from the operations staff, or both?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, if you could, sir - and I will only do this on this one document - if you could -- or if the ELMO could be zoomed out and perhaps zoomed in onto the text at the upper left. If it could be moved down, please, the document. Okay. If we could now zoom in on the text at the middle on the left-hand side. And the document could be moved in a little bit more. That's fine. Sir, do you see on the left-hand side the typewritten script with -- immediately below "Command of the 3rd Corps"? Where there's an abbreviation STR. Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That means strictly confidential. I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following that, sir, are a number -- or is a number. Do you see the number?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- well, first of all, that identifying number has really three components. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's the number before the slash, the number after the slash, and the number after the dash. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what those three numbers refer to or what their purpose is? Let's start with the first one, if you remember. 02, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: 02 means that the document was prepared by the deputy commander. So it's not quite clear to me, but probably he was absent and that is why I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you sure that the 02 does not indicate that the staff prepared the document, someone within the staff?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The operations department is part of the staff, so I'm not at all sure whether they may have prepared this document, but it must be on the orders of the deputy commander who gave them the information on the basis of which they drew up the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn to the second component, that is the number after the slash, and in this instance that's number 33. Do you see the number 33?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of that second number is?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: 33 should be an identification number that it was given in the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be correct, sir, to say that that second number, in this case number 33, sets forth the function of the document in question?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back, then. You've told us that it has to do with a log. Is that what you said, that the second number deals with a log?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many different types of logs were employed within the 3rd Corps? How many types of logs did they have?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how many there were, but I know that everybody in the corps when it was formed, when the administration was set up, would be given a list with their own identification number. So all documents should have used that identification number. And the number of the document itself is the last number here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So the -- and this document, the number 1341, would simply be a serial, a sequential number that would be assigned to all the documents --

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, an ordinal number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's an ordinal number to all the documents falling within the category of 33?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it from what you told us that each department had its own number. Is that what the second number would refer to?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is what it means. The logistics had their numbers, security and protection had their number, intelligence had their number. So these were branches and services. The chief of communications, artillery, infantry, each had their own number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that that document -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before I do that, sir, could you tell me in general what type of document this is.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The document would belong to the group of documents for control and command, because in this document, as far as I can see from the heading as I can't see the rest of the text, comments on a report received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd ask that that document be returned and that contested document 573 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask that you -- with respect to the next few documents, I'm going to be asking if you recognise the signature, so perhaps on this document if you could -- if it could be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I do. This is also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, this is a situation where you've signed on behalf of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably he was absent. And I saw the first page, and the content of the document is quite beyond my area of activity. It's a political document, if I can call it that. It isn't an operational document. But as the commander wasn't there, I probably signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask now that that document be returned and that the witness be shown contested document 546.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I'd focus your attention on the signature. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, this stamp next to your signature appears to be different from some of the other stamps we've seen. Do you happen to have any information or knowledge about this stamp?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say unless perhaps I could see the date of this document, because we changed the stamps in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. The original is on the machine immediately to your left. If perhaps the usher could turn it over so that we could see the date, or you could actually look at the date on the document.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I see. So I was right. This is -- this was the first version of the stamp. Could you turn it back again so I could see the stamp. Probably at first we thought that this would be sufficient, just the indication "3rd Corps." However, later on, the people from the general services, probably on orders from the commander, changed it. So we made it more up-to-date and more meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would again ask that that document be returned and that the witness be shown contested document 433.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can barely be seen on the screen, but I signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, if you could actually physically perhaps take the original. Again, sir, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again with the assistance of the usher, I'd ask that that document be returned and that contested --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- I do apologise. Once again there is an indication 02. So it means that I signed on behalf of the person who was supposed to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask that the witness now be shown contested document 649.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the document. My bodies drafted it and I'd signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'd now ask that the witness be shown contested document 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document or the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I recognise the signature, but I can't say I can be sure about the document, it was so long ago, but again there is 02 on it, which means that the person was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: May that document be returned. I have one final document to show the witness. This is contested document 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the signature on this document or the markings, the handwritten markings?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: These are initials. The deputy commander, Dzemal Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that that document be returned, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mekic, the Prosecution appreciates you answering our questions both in Sarajevo and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no further questions for the witness at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's almost time for the technical break, so it's better that we have the break now, and then I'll give the floor to the Defence. It is almost twenty-five past twelve, so we'll resume at five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without wasting any time, I'll give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Mekic. We have already met, but for the sake of the transcript I will introduce myself. My name is Edina Residovic and I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I would be grateful if you would answer a number of questions that have to do with the questions put to you by my learned colleague from the Prosecution. You gave lengthy answers to my learned colleague and said that the conditions -- the working conditions when creating the 3rd Corps were very difficult, and you also stated that you didn't have adequate communications equipment and that you had problems as far as electricity was concerned, the use of equipment was concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, would it be correct to say, Mr. Mekic, that even the communications equipment that you were able to obtain was difficult to use because the radio and other devices were under an embargo, just like weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, you said that you did your best to organise a system for transmitting your orders and other documents or, rather, for the reception of those documents and within the staff of which you were the chief, and you had an assistant for communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This communications assistant was involved in planning and organising the communications system within the 3rd Corps in those difficult conditions, and within the staff there was also a communications company which in fact was involved in receiving and sending documents from the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That communications centre, as well as the operations centre, were organised in such a manner that they worked on a 24-hour basis and links with subordinate units were provided to the best of your ability, although at times this was almost impossible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first slightly more stable and secure communications system, the so-called Paket communications, was established when you received a modem which you connected to a computer and a radio, and sometime in March 1993, you established a regular link with the Supreme Command Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And on the other side they had something, because on both sides you need the same equipment to have such a link. And I think we received a computer, which gave us much joy. And towards the end of March I think we established a link, a communications link, to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just answered my next question. The process of establishing -- there was a process for establishing a link with subordinate units, because first you had to find the equipment, the radios, the modems, and computers in brigades, and it was then necessary to train staff to operate these devices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In that communications company, the chief of communications organised training sessions and trained men, trained the personnel to do that work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You briefly spoke about various difficulties that you faced, but as this is not the subject of this discussion, I'll just ask you whether it would be correct to say that as the chief of the 3rd Corps staff you spent a significant part of time on training the staff, administrative staff and communications staff, because as you said, your staff resources were very meager when you started the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And as you are well aware in the 3rd Corps Command - or perhaps you're not aware of this - we established a military officers school so we would train our own personnel because we really didn't have the necessary personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to those problems that you have mentioned, and you have just confirmed that those problems existed in answer to my questions, when communicating with subordinate units, you had significant problems because messages were jammed since the HVO had taken over a very powerful device from the JNA which they used to very efficiently jam messages transmitted from the 3rd Corps to subordinate units and from subordinate units to the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the major tasks one has in wartime. Jamming is one of the major tasks. And this is what they did on all frequencies more or less. We weren't able to get through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear to the Trial Chamber that you had problems in the 3rd corps as far as transmitting and receiving orders are concerned, but Mr. Mekic, would it be correct to say that the problems increased the lower the level of the unit concerned? So brigades and battalions and others more or less had to depend on traditional career lines, if that's how we could put it.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: If we had one computer in the corps, well, you can imagine what the situation was in a brigade or a company or a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke in detail about how the 3rd Corps, or, rather, in the staff drafts -- orders were drafted, and I think that you also mentioned that there was a -- a long and a short procedure for preparing orders. If I followed you correctly in response to a question from my colleague, you explained how the most complicated orders were drafted. Naturally such orders are combat orders or orders to defend or attack. And if I have understood this correctly, all the elements within the staff were included in analysing and preparing a suggestion for the commander's order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These orders were very lengthy, and they contained all the essential elements; an assessment of the enemy forces, of your own forces, an assessment of the tasks for your own units. They addressed the necessity of respecting the Geneva Conventions. They addressed the issue of prisoners of war, et cetera, et cetera. So these were very complete orders that were prepared in your staff, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The full method was always followed when drafting combat documents and orders. This was always done when we had enough time. The short procedure was followed when we didn't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When discussing these various difficulties, you would agree that in 1993 -- 1993 was the most difficult year in that war, and tell me, at that time, did you in the corps often have to violate the instructions that you have already mentioned, not respect those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, the situation was the most difficult situation. What do you do when you receive a report that from the direction of Zepce and Sahere [phoen] towards Zenica there are 25.000 refugees, women, children, the elderly, et cetera, et cetera? In such a situation, it is necessary to react very rapidly and see how to deal with the situation to avoid any further complications, because naturally the other side knew what they were doing, and these people were fleeing because of them. So we would have to deal with them, and they take advantage of the situation to create a tragedy at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't go into details, but you provide an example of the situation you were in, and you told us why you would sometimes work and follow a shorter procedure. Thank you for that answer. As far as what happened to the orders is concerned, the orders that you provided to subordinate units, operation groups or brigades to which the order was addressed, you in the 3rd Corps did not have the possibility of monitoring how the brigade itself would forward this order to the troops via battalions, et cetera. Isn't that correct? You didn't have a system that could monitor that apart from the fact that you would later have reports from those brigades about how the order was implemented?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Until we received a report we couldn't even be sure that the unit in question received the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it also be correct to say, Mr. Mekic, that the 3rd Corps Command didn't have, according to the regulations or in reality, any insight into orders, documents, or reports that circulated in lower subordinate units? In fact, if a platoon sent something to a company or to -- or if a battalion was informing its platoon about something, the 3rd Corps never received such documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this isn't supposed to happen, according to the system of control or command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the technique itself is concerned, you said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that when a commander signs a document he goes to the general services office or to the protocol office. The document is then registered there, it is stamped or, rather, one of the stamps is used to stamp that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, have I understand you correctly, that the person who signs the document doesn't have a stamp with him? The stamp's in a room in the protocol office, and the people who work in the protocol office are those who have certified the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You have understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document is then sent from that service to the communications centre, and would it be correct to say that communications personnel would only check to see whether the document has a stamp and a signature, and they don't have the authority to check to see whether this is actually the person who signed the document and whether the person in the protocol office was authorised to stamp the document or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had one other question for you. Yes. You mentioned the rules that should be followed, and also you said that, in reality, the rules were often not followed because personnel wasn't sufficiently trained, they weren't sufficiently professional, et cetera, et cetera. However, would it be correct that neither you nor the commander, given the situation you were in in 1993, were able to pay a lot of attention to those issues at the time? You couldn't check to see whether a document had been correctly signed or whether it had correctly stamped, because life was such that you were not in a position to carry out such checks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my very last question: You would agree with me that the position of the corps commander in all armies, including our own, is a very high-ranking position, and the commanders are involved in strategy and planning and organisation at that level, and they are not very involved in specific -- in the specific duties of the staff officer, et cetera. So his main duty is to see the overall picture, and it was your task to analyse it and make suggestions to the commander as to how certain problems should be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: The commander -- well, depending on the number of brigades he had, that's the number of subordinate officers he had. So it's the brigade commander who is the first person who is held accountable by that commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mekic, for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, but first of all I would like to point out to the Defence that on page 34, line 13, you said it is clear to the Trial Chamber that you had a problem as far as the transmission and reception of orders is concerned. This is a claim made by the Defence, but the Trial Chamber doesn't share this opinion, because at this point in time we don't have any convictions as far as the stated proposition is concerned, but you claimed that the Trial Chamber was persuaded that there was a problem. Perhaps it's a translation problem, a problem when translating from B/C/S into English, but that's what is stated in line 13 on page 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was obviously my mistake. It wasn't a translation mistake. I wanted to say that it was clear that when answering questions put to him by my colleagues, the witness provided enough information about problems for the Trial Chamber. I apologise if I gave the impression that the Trial Chamber had drawn any conclusions because that is not my position and that's not something that I would do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you can see, the Trial Chamber is paying a lot of attention to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, just a minor question. You've almost answered all the questions of a technical nature that have been put to you and we would like to thank you for having clarified certain issues. If you don't mind, I'm going to ask document 41 to be shown to you again. We can put it on the ELMO. As far as the stamp is concerned, the stamp at the bottom of the document, you said that there were three types of stamps. We saw one a minute ago. This stamp seems to come from the beginning of 1993. This stamp here is of a different kind. I would like you to clear a slight -- clear up a slight matter, because I see the number 3 above the word "corps" in the stamp. This number 3, does it indicate the person who is third in command in hierarchy? Does it mean that there is a stamp number 1 for the 3rd Corps commander; a stamp number 2 for the deputy, that is to say for Mr. Merdan; and a stamp number 3 for you, the chief of staff; or does number 3 also mean or indicate the 3rd Corps? Could you clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should be. However, three stamps were in existence. For the sake of security, they were kept in a metal cupboard, and there is only one example of each. There weren't three types of stamps, or perhaps I haven't understood you correctly. There was one type of stamp but with numbers 1, 2, and 3. And each stamp means the same thing and it was impossible to control everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be more precise. For example, if the 3rd Corps commander drafts a document himself, he signs it himself, the stamp used on the document, would it be the same stamp that we have here but instead of number 3 would it be necessary for this stamp to have number 1 on it?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion that's how it should be, but I'm not sure that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will show you a document now, a document that I was able to examine during the break, in order to enable you to illustrate this issue, but I have to find it first. As you have the document before you, when it says 02 in the left-hand corner, does this mean that the person who drafted the document is number 2 in that hierarchy, in the chain of command? In this case it would be Mr. Merdan. If you yourself have drafted a document, the number wouldn't be 02, the number would be 03; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So when 02 drafts a document, for example, Mr. Merdan would be the person who drafts the document, would he first of all discuss this with number 1, that is to say the 3rd Corps commander, in order to find out whether he agreed with the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: As a rule, yes, if the commander was present in the corps command at the time. Perhaps he was in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As a rule, he discusses it. If number 2 isn't there at the time, is he going to ask number 3 to sign on his behalf? Because the document that you have before you, which was signed not by yourself but by Mr. Merdan, since you have recognised the signature, in such a case is the person who is above, does he ask the person below him to sign on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule if the situation makes this possible, yes. But perhaps the commander was in the field at the time so he wasn't even aware of this, and the situation was such that it was urgent to do this. In such a case, he couldn't ask him to sign on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you signed for the 3rd Corps commander, because we know that you did sign on behalf of the 3rd Corps commander, when you signed document number 2, Mr. Merdan was certainly not there, otherwise he would have signed the document. Number 1 was perhaps not there either, which means that the most high-ranking officer in the 3rd Corps was you yourself. The most high-ranking officer present in the 3rd Corps was you.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do agree that if you sign a document, that means that the others aren't present, because if they are present, they should sign the documents. Is this how the issue of signing documents was regulated?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that those are the sort of unwritten rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the person who signed the document must first check that the person who should sign isn't present, because you know that when one signs a document, one is assuming a certain responsibility. To sign a document is not a neutral act. It has certain consequences. So when you sign a document, you are aware of the fact that the person who should usually sign the document isn't present there. Or were there cases in which you were -- in which the person who drafted the order was present but asked you to sign on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, I or perhaps the second person in command couldn't take any decisions if agreement had not been reached. If the commander ordered something should be done, if he was in the field but he had said that certain measures should be taken and if he had said how units should be informed, in such cases his order would be followed. But we always knew -- if I was in the field, he knew where I was and vice versa. Mr. -- that was also the case for Mr. Merdan. If Mr. Merdan was visiting units, if the three of us were in the field, we made sure that there was someone present, and that's why on occasion there are also signatures that are not the signatures of the three of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the registrar have document 442 that is contested? Very well. We will show this document. Could you place it on the ELMO, please, so that everyone can see it. Please just have a look at the stamp. Have a look at the stamp. Can you see that there is the number 3 on this stamp, and you can see the signature. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Hadzihasanovic's signature, the commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So how is it that we don't have number 1 on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Again, as I said, this was up to the secretary who worked in the general services office. It was up to that person to use a stamp. I can't tell you exactly why number 1 isn't on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order, of which we have an original, when it is signed by the 3rd Corps commander in person, as far as I understand, he doesn't stamp the document. Can you confirm that it isn't the person who signs the document who stamps the document.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the order is taken to the communications company since the communications company will forward the order, and it is there in the protocol office that an officer or soldier stamps the order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In theory, the soldier who stamps the document must have the three stamps; stamp number 1, stamp number 2, and stamp number 3. If it's his superior commander who is signing, he should use the stamp number 1. He shouldn't make any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you can't explain the fact that stamp number 3 was used in this case?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I can't explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will take the document back. Very well. I have no further questions. Any other questions for Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have one question. Could the witness be shown DH109. DH109 ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could be placed on the ELMO. I will give the witness my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll place it on the ELMO. Everyone can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mekic, could you please have a look at this document. As you said a minute ago, you think that these are the initials of General Merdan, the deputy commander, and this is his signature?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that he was the person who used stamp number 2. Could you have a look at this document and say whether this is the correct procedure that the administration office should follow when using a stamp? You can have a look at the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Is this number 2? I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the stamp there is a number 2, as far as I can see. But you have a look.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Could you zoom in a bit, please? Yes, it is number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: This would be the correct procedure to be followed when processing combat documents, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can return the document to me. And there is one other document I would like to show the witness; DH110. I would like the witness to comment on a number. You can return that document to me, and there is another document. Could you please show it to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please just have a look at the number, 03/100, and could you please explain the number for us. And once you have had a look at the document, could you place it on the ELMO. Would you please put the document on the ELMO, please. Will you look at the number on top. It says 03, though it is the security sector. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So my question is, for the sake of clarity, when you spoke a moment ago about 03, you didn't have in mind you personally but the staff. So this number 03 before the dash -- the slash, is the body as a whole and not an individual officer who signs the document.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: This number doesn't relate to an individual but to a body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And finally, in view of all those problems, you were aware that some confusion may have occurred in the use of the stamps and deviation from the rules regarding office work when documents were registered?

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: I think that is something I have already said. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is signed. It is a specialist document. It is signed by the head of the security sector, and it is his duty to put down his name and to sign it because it has to do with security.

utterances.speaker: MURADIF MEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we have just noted that the parties and the Judges have finished with their questions. We thank you for coming to The Hague to testify about certain technical aspects relating to stamps and documents. We thank you again for coming to testify. We wish you a safe journey home and best wishes for your retirement. I would like to ask Madam Usher to be kind enough to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
